setupSteps: Sit down first, then pick up the handle. Sit on the seat facing the stack. Sources warn against grabbing a heavy handle, standing on one foot and "plopping" down, which jerks the back.

Feet: put the whole foot flat on the foot plate, hip-width apart, with the plate at a height where your feet rest comfortably (several guides say adjust the seat or plate so the feet sit comfortably).

Knees: a slight bend, not locked; FitPlate target knee angle about 130–165 degrees (hip–knee–ankle, est.). If your feet slide or the knees lock out, reset before adding weight (one guide's advice). No clinical knee-angle standard was found.

Distance: adjust so that, with arms straight and a tall back, you feel a light stretch in the back without being pulled forward off the seat. Some machines have a fixed plate; sit further back or forward on the seat.
V-handle (close grip, neutral palms facing each other): FitPlate start. Clip it to the cable hook and check the gate is closed and the handle is not cracked.
Straight or wide bar: hands about shoulder-width or wider, overhand. Sources link this to more mid-back and rear-shoulder work. Use it once the V-handle is smooth.
Check the cable: look for fraying or a stuck pulley; tell staff if damaged (common practice; no formal standard found).

Choose a light load first. Insert the pin in the lowest or second-lowest plate. One guide advises checking your form before you put the pin in and start pulling; do this with the handle and no load if the machine allows.
Push the pin all the way in so it cannot fall out; re-check before you pull.
If the plates are unmarked or in different units, ask staff; do not guess.
Torso: sit tall with the chest up and ribs down, the natural curve of the lower back kept (ACE: keep the natural arch and brace the abs, but do not press the low back flat or arch hard).
Shoulders: down and back, away from the ears; wrists in line with the forearms (ACE).

Start (getting the handle): with a heavier stack, sit with the knees bent, hold the handle with both hands and lean forward only as far as needed to pick it up, then sit tall as the cable takes load. If the load is too heavy to sit up with, reduce the weight; ask staff or a friend to hand you the handle.
Do not yank the handle to start the first rep; start with a smooth pull.

End (putting it back): after the last rep, let the arms extend slowly while the stack settles, lean forward slightly, bend the knees more to reduce tension, and place the handle on the stack bracket or let it return under control. Do not release the handle while the arms are straight and the cable is under full tension, because it can snap back toward the pulley.
If you cannot finish a rep: bring the handle to your lower ribs, keep the back tall, and lower the handle slowly while bending the knees to slacken the cable; do not drop it.

steps.title: Set the pin and seat
steps.action: Put the pin in a light plate, sit down, and put both feet on the foot plate.
steps.visualCheck: Side: feet flat, knees slightly bent. Front: feet hip-width.

steps.title: Take the handle and sit tall
steps.action: Take the V-handle with both hands, palms facing each other, and sit tall with a long spine.
steps.feel: Light tension through the arms; abs braced.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back straight, chest up, no rounding.

steps.title: Set the start position
steps.action: Let the arms straighten forward without letting the back round; the shoulder blades may glide slightly forward.
steps.feel: A mild stretch across the upper back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: arms nearly straight (elbows not locked), torso only slightly forward of vertical (est. up to 15 degrees).

steps.title: Start with the shoulder blades
steps.action: Draw the shoulder blades back and down first.
steps.feel: The muscles between the shoulder blades switch on.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders do not rise toward the ears.

steps.title: Pull the elbows back
steps.action: Drive the elbows back past the sides of the body, keeping them close, and pull the handle toward the lower ribs or belly.
steps.visualCheck: Side: the elbows travel back in a straight line; the torso stays upright with at most a small lean.

steps.title: Squeeze
steps.action: Hold when the handle touches the lower ribs; keep the chest up.
steps.feel: A firm squeeze between the shoulder blades.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbows about level with or just behind the torso; no leaning back past vertical.

steps.title: Return slowly
steps.action: Let the arms extend slowly, with the shoulder blades gliding forward last.
steps.feel: Back stretching under control; stack not slamming.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back stays straight; plates do not touch the rest of the stack.

steps.title: Repeat, then finish
steps.action: Repeat steps 4–7. After the last rep, extend the arms slowly and put the handle back as in section 3, point 15.
steps.visualCheck: The handle returns to the pulley or rack without snapping back.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning back to swing the weight
commonMistakes.text: Leaning back to swing the weight. Why: the lower back takes load, the back muscles lose tension; several sources call it the most common error. Fix: lighter weight, torso still, stop the lean at vertical.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back at the stretch
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back at the stretch. Why: loads the spine and discs in a flexed position. Fix: sit tall, stop the stretch before the back rounds, let only the shoulder blades move forward.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling with the arms and hands
commonMistakes.text: Pulling with the arms and hands. Why: the biceps do the work and the back stays quiet. Fix: start by drawing the shoulder blades back, then lead with the elbows.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging the shoulders
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging the shoulders. Why: the upper trapezius takes over and the neck tightens. Fix: shoulders away from the ears.

commonMistakes.title: Too much weight
commonMistakes.text: Too much weight. Why: causes swinging, rounded back and short range. Fix: choose a load you can control for 10–12 reps with 3–4 reps left (see section 7).

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knees or letting the feet slide
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knees or letting the feet slide. Why: the back takes extra load and you lose your base. Fix: soft knees, whole foot on the plate.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling the handle too high or too low
commonMistakes.text: Pulling the handle too high or too low. Why: changes the muscles worked and encourages leaning. Fix: lower ribs.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the stack slam or the handle snap back
commonMistakes.text: Letting the stack slam or the handle snap back. Why: jerky loading, noise and risk of injury. Fix: a controlled 3-second return; follow section 3, point 15.

commonMistakes.title: Plopping down with a heavy load
commonMistakes.text: Plopping down with a heavy load. Why: jerks the spine. Fix: sit first, light load, use the correct hand-off.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing the stretch
commonMistakes.text: Rushing the stretch. Why: control is lost in the lengthening half. Fix: 3 seconds back, 2 seconds pull.

safetyNotes: Lower back pain: the move needs a still spine; use light loads, a tall back and a short range; a chest-supported row or lat pulldown may suit better. If pain persists, ask a professional (one article notes that some people cannot do seated cable rows because of back pain).
Shoulder problems: use a shorter range, a lighter load, and avoid pulling the elbows far behind the body.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; breathe out on the pull.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table; ask a professional.

Note: all sources for this item were seen only as search-result summaries (pages not opened in full); most are coaching blogs and exercise libraries. The 150/90 degree elbow thresholds, the 15 degree torso-lean limit, the 120–170 degree knee band, the pull-to-lower-ribs target and the sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: a controlled EMG study comparing V-handle with wide-bar rows or trunk lean; a professional-body guide for handle return; a clinical shoulder or spine range limit; a sample starting load in kg; condition-specific sources for knee pain, shoulder problems, obesity and PCOS; foot-plate and knee-angle standards.
